Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette:
Robert, a fifty-three-year-old social worker, had always prided himself on his unwavering dedication and his ability to connect with people from all walks of life. His work often took him into unfamiliar neighborhoods and various homes, a reality he embraced until a little over two years ago. He had been conducting a routine home visit in a somewhat run-down apartment building, a new client referral in a part of the city he hadn't frequented much. The client, a man in his late twenties, had seemed agitated but cooperative. Robert was asked to step into a small, windowless back room to review some paperwork, a common enough request. It was in that confined space, the door clicking shut behind him, that the world shifted irrevocably. The assault was sudden, brutal, and overwhelming, leaving him disoriented and numb.

In the immediate aftermath, a profound sense of terror clung to him, a cold, visceral dread that resurfaced whenever he revisited the memory. Remembering the event brought back the same terror he felt at the time, a heart-pounding, breath-stealing re-experience. Compounding this was an intense shame that washed over him whenever the details intruded, a burning humiliation that made him recoil from his own thoughts. He knew what had happened, the sequence of events, the actions taken, yet when he tried to articulate it, to put words to the experience, he found himself utterly unable. The words simply wouldn't come, a jumble of raw feeling and fragmented images, leaving him frustrated and isolated in his struggle to convey the depth of his ordeal.

Over the following months, Robert's world began to shrink. The memory of that small, enclosed room became a potent trigger. He started actively avoiding enclosed or confined spaces, opting for the stairs over elevators in his office building, making excuses to hold meetings in larger, open-plan areas, and finding himself increasingly uncomfortable in client homes with narrow hallways or small rooms. His once adventurous spirit, which had allowed him to navigate the city's diverse landscape for his job, was replaced by a pervasive caution. He now avoided going to unfamiliar places, convinced he could no longer accurately assess the danger, which significantly hampered his ability to take on new client referrals outside his established routes.

A new vigilance settled over him. When walking to his car after a late appointment, or even just through the office parking lot, he frequently looked behind him to check if someone was following him, a constant, low-level hum of anxiety accompanying his movements. This hyper-awareness extended to his expectations of others; when something took longer than expected-a colleague's delay in responding to an email, a client running late for an appointment-he would immediately assume something bad was happening, his mind leaping to worst-case scenarios involving danger or harm.

In an attempt to regain a sense of control, Robert began to ruminate about how to get even with his assailant, replaying scenarios in his mind, imagining confrontations, devising elaborate plans for retribution. These thoughts offered a fleeting sense of power, but ultimately left him exhausted and consumed. Simultaneously, he fiercely tried to push the intrusive thoughts and memories of the assault out of his mind, a constant internal battle to suppress the images and feelings that threatened to overwhelm him. He would try to distract himself with work, with household chores, anything to keep the memories at bay, but they always returned.

His professional life, once a source of deep satisfaction, became increasingly fraught. His reluctance to enter new homes or small consultation rooms meant he was subtly shifting his caseload, favoring clients in familiar settings, and turning down opportunities for professional growth that would require him to venture into new environments. His supervisor had begun to notice his decreased flexibility, though Robert offered vague explanations. At home, his wife noticed his increasing preoccupation and withdrawal, the way he would suddenly go quiet, lost in thought, or the way he now insisted on taking specific, well-lit routes, even if they were longer. The constant internal struggle and the relentless threat monitoring left him perpetually on edge, making it difficult to fully engage with her.

It was the realization that his professional effectiveness was severely compromised, coupled with a growing sense of isolation from his wife, that finally led Robert to seek help. He knew he couldn't continue living this way, constantly scanning for danger, trapped by memories, and consumed by thoughts of revenge or desperate suppression. What frightened him most was the thought of losing himself entirely to this pervasive dread, of becoming a shell of the social worker and husband he once was.
